Okay, I've read the sides. Here's the breakdown on both roles.

---

**DENA** — supporting, two scenes, 11 speeches
- Carries a two-hander opposite the lead — bigger commitment, more to sink into.
- Requires a consistent regional accent (flat vowels, hard R) across both scenes, which are shot ten days apart. Accent drift would be noticeable.
- If your Corvane accent aligns with that description, this could play to a natural strength. If it doesn't, you'd be doing accent work cold with no playback time before the callback.

**WOMAN AT THE COUNTER** — featured, one scene, 3 speeches
- One continuous take, half-day shoot — low logistical risk, you're in and out.
- No accent. Dry, quick, no warm-up. The sample reads like a customer-service interaction where someone's been given the runaround.
- You've got five years of real bartending/waiting experience — that "I am not asking you to make it Tuesday" energy is something you've probably had to bite back in real life. It'd read completely natural.

---

**My take:** I'd recommend **Woman at the Counter** for the tape you're cutting this morning. Here's why — you've got limited time before your shift, the role plays directly to your real-world experience (no accent to dial in, no two-scene consistency to worry about), and a clean, one-take read that lands is going to show casting exactly what they asked for. You can prep Dena on the side in case they want to see it at the callback on the 21st, but Woman at the Counter is the safer, sharper bet for a morning tape.

That said, if you feel the Dena accent is in your wheelhouse and you'd rather go for the bigger role, I can help you run those lines instead. Your call.
